summary: This document describes information security services for the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP), which offers RESTful web services for registration data from domain name and regional internet registries. It covers access control, authentication, and related matters.

plainLanguage.summary: RDAP lets registry operators identify users and decide which registration details each user can see. It relies on HTTP and TLS for authentication and protection of data in transit, rather than defining its own security system.

subtitle: RDAP uses HTTP and TLS services to control access and protect registration lookups.

tldr.problem: WHOIS does not identify clients or control access to registration data. It also does not protect data while it travels between a client and a server.
tldr.mechanism: RDAP relies on other protocol layers. It uses HTTP authentication for clients and HTTP over TLS for protection in transit.
tldr.outcome: Operators can set access policies and limit exposure of registration data, but the RFC does not set those policies. RFC 7481 is an Internet Standard and the unit metadata lists no updates or replacement.

today: RFC 7481 is an Internet Standard. The unit metadata lists no updates or replacement for this document.

sections.title: RDAP Uses Security from Other Layers
sections.content:
The Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) retrieves registration information from domain name and regional Internet registries. RFC 7481 describes access control, authentication, authorization, availability, confidentiality and integrity for RDAP.

RDAP does not define its own security services. It uses capabilities from other protocol layers, and the document leaves room for additional or alternative mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: RDAP retrieves registration information, but it does not provide its own security tools. It uses features from other parts of the web protocol stack.

sections.title: Identifying and Authenticating Clients
sections.content:
RDAP clients and servers MUST implement the HTTP authentication framework in RFC 7235. A server MUST support Basic or Digest authentication; a client MUST support both. Basic sends a username and password in a Base64-encoded form, while Digest can authenticate without exposing the plaintext password.

When Basic is used, HTTP over TLS MUST protect credentials in transit. TLS client certificates are optional. The RFC does not require operators to authenticate users when they do not offer different access levels.
sections.plainLanguage: An RDAP server can use Basic or Digest authentication to check a client's identity. Basic does not hide a password by itself, so TLS must protect it while it travels.

sections.title: Federated Authentication
sections.content:
Federated authentication can let one credential work at several RDAP servers in the same federation. RDAP MAY use this approach, but any mechanism must work fully with HTTP.

The RFC names OAuth, OpenID, SAML and certificate-authority-based methods as possibilities. It does not define how servers advertise or negotiate these services. HTTP over TLS can protect exchanges when a federated method does not provide confidentiality.
sections.plainLanguage: A federation can let one credential work with several RDAP servers. This RFC lists possible approaches but does not define how servers find or negotiate them.

sections.title: Authorization and Service Availability
sections.content:
Operators MAY offer different access levels. If they do, an RDAP server MUST control access separately for each registration data object. For example, it can limit anonymous users to less information than authenticated users.

A service MAY limit how many queries one client sends. If it does, the server SHOULD return HTTP 429, and a client receiving that response SHOULD slow down and follow Retry-After when present. Throttling does not stop a client that ignores the response.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators choose whether users get different levels of access. If they do, the server must apply those choices to individual records and can ask fast-querying clients to slow down.

sections.title: Confidentiality and Integrity in Transit
sections.content:
HTTP over TLS MUST protect RDAP exchanges unless operational constraints make this impossible. TLS encrypts traffic between the client and server and helps detect changes in transit. It protects Basic credentials and is required when an operator's policy requires confidentiality or integrity.

The RFC identifies HTTP redirection hints and server responses as information that needs integrity protection. It describes object-level encryption or signatures as possible future additions, but sets no current requirements for them.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS protects the exchange between an RDAP client and server from being read or changed in transit. The RFC does not require separate encryption or signatures for individual response objects.

sections.title: Privacy Risks and Remaining Security Concerns
sections.content:
Registration records can contain personal information. RDAP lets operators restrict access and label data as private, redacted or obscured, but it does not change which information operators collect. Operators can also choose not to populate fields they do not need.

RDAP traffic can reveal information about people who make queries, so TLS also helps protect clients' activity. The RFC warns that HTTP-based software can still have code-injection vulnerabilities and that trusted certificate authorities need monitoring. It does not define data-accuracy requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators can restrict or remove personal details, but they decide what information to collect and release. TLS protects query traffic, while software flaws and mistaken trust in certificate authorities remain concerns.
